requirement_title: Feature Request: Allow generation of Formatter for a type in a referenced assembly
requirement_text:
# REQ-2129: Feature Request: Allow generation of Formatter for a type in a referenced assembly

Source: https://github.com/MessagePack-CSharp/MessagePack-CSharp/issues/2129
Type: feature

## Requirement

Given Project A (contains `ProjectA.MyType`, has no and cannot have a reference to the MessagePack NuGet package) and Project B (references Project A and MessagePack), the reporter needs a source-generated `IMessagePackFormatter` for `ProjectA.MyType` generated inside Project B.

Proposed solution: add a `[GeneratedMessagePackFormatter]` attribute that works for partial classes implementing `IMessagePackFormatter<T>`:

```csharp
[GeneratedMessagePackFormatter]
partial class MyObjectFormatter: IMessagePackFormatter<MyObject>;
```

The class does not need a body; the implementation is source-generated by `MessagePack.SourceGenerator.MessagePackGenerator` as usual.

For attribute-based property keys and other settings (such as Union), the issue lists three alternatives: (1) use `System.Runtime.Serialization.DataMember` and related attributes; (2) let the generator and analyzers work with user-defined copies of the MessagePack attributes; (3) source-generate the attributes themselves via `RegisterPostInitializationOutput`.

Motivation: Project A is a NuGet library that should stay minimal with zero dependencies.

## Acceptance criteria

- A `[GeneratedMessagePackFormatter]` attribute exists and can be applied to a partial class implementing `IMessagePackFormatter<T>`.
- The source generator emits the formatter implementation for `T` inside the annotated class, in the assembly that declares the class (Project B), even when `T` is declared in a referenced assembly.
- The annotated class may be declared without a body (`partial class X : IMessagePackFormatter<T>;`).
- `T` needs no MessagePack attributes: without `[DataContract]` or `[MessagePackObject]` on `T` the generated formatter uses contractless behaviour over public members. (derived from maintainer comment)
- If `T` does carry MessagePack attributes, they are honoured. (derived from maintainer comment)
- Private members are not required to be serialized; only public members are in scope. (derived from maintainer comment)
- Project A needs no reference to the MessagePack package. (derived)

## Notes from discussion

- AArnott: "We might simplistically say this only works in 'contractless' mode, such that you need no attributes on it at all. If there are attributes on it, fine, we'll use them. But if there is no `[DataContract]` or `[MessagePackObject]` attribute on the type, go contractless by default."
- AArnott on prerequisite: "Does ProjectA.MyType requires only `public` members to be serialized? That seems a prerequisite for anything here." Reporter: yes.
- AArnott is not a fan of a `PropertyKeys` dictionary on the formatter, and warns that copying attributes into Project A breaks reflection-based (dynamic resolver) mode.
- AArnott suggested a surrogate-type design: `[GeneratedMessagePackFormatter(SurrogateType = typeof(ProjectASurrogate))]`, keys mapped by property name; reporter: "Looks good." No design was settled in the thread.

findings.claim: The requirement says MessagePack attributes on T must be honoured, but without a surrogate the collector ignores every attribute on T. It always calls CreateContractlessMembers, which never reads [MessagePackObject], [Key], [IgnoreMember], [DataContract], [DataMember] or [IgnoreDataMember]. The result: a member T marks [IgnoreMember] is still serialized, [Key(int)] keys become string keys named after the members, and [DataContract] types serialize undeclared public members.

receipt_plan.detail: Run Receipts.GeneratedTests.GeneratedFormatterHonoursTypeAttributesTests (IgnoreMemberOnReferencedMessagePackObjectIsHonoured, DataContractOnReferencedTypeIsHonoured). On head the generated formatter still references 'SecretValue', so both fail.

findings.claim: The requirement says MessagePack attributes on T must be honoured, but they are ignored. In contractless mode the collector never reads T's attributes: CreateContractlessMembers takes every public read-write member, sorts it by name and gives it a string key. For a metadata type with [MessagePackObject], [Key(0)] Id and [IgnoreMember] Secret, the generated formatter writes a string-keyed map with 'Id' and also serializes 'Secret', which T explicitly excluded. The wire format also differs from T's own formatter.

receipt_plan.detail: Run Receipts.GeneratedTests.GeneratedFormatterLogicReceiptsTests.AttributesOnFormattedTypeAreHonoured. ProjectA.MyType (emitted to metadata) has [MessagePackObject], [Key(0)] Id and [IgnoreMember] Secret. The generated MyTypeFormatter source contains 'Secret' on head.

findings.claim: In surrogate mode every instance field or property of the surrogate, including private ones, must carry [Key] or [IgnoreMember]. Otherwise MemberNeedsKey is reported and no formatter is generated. A normal [MessagePackObject] surrogate with a private helper field is therefore rejected, although the regular analyzer only requires keys on public members (L5).

findings.claim: A surrogate declared [MessagePackObject(true)] (keyAsPropertyName, L3) needs no [Key] attributes. The surrogate collector still demands a Key on every member, so it reports MemberNeedsKey and generates nothing. The keyAsPropertyName argument is never read, which contradicts the documented 'every MessagePack attribute on the surrogate is honoured'.

receipt_plan.detail: Run GeneratedFormatterLogicReceiptsTests.KeyAsPropertyNameSurrogateIsAccepted. The run result has a MemberNeedsKey diagnostic on head.

hunches.claim: Contractless mode here covers only public read-write members and a parameterless constructor. Get-only public properties are silently dropped from serialization. Types that have only a parameterized constructor are rejected with NoDeserializingConstructor (constructorParameters is always empty). The existing contractless resolver serializes readable members and matches constructor parameters, so 'contractless behaviour over public members' is only partly delivered for immutable library types.

receipt_plan.detail: Use the generator harness with a ProjectA type `public class P { public P(int id) { Id = id; } public int Id { get; } }` and a bodyless [GeneratedMessagePackFormatter] for it. Expect on head: a NoDeserializingConstructor diagnostic and no formatter. Then compare with DynamicContractlessObjectResolver, which round-trips P.

hunches.claim: Generated formatter models are added to the same model set whose output is gated by Options.IsGeneratingSource. If the project declares no [GeneratedMessagePackResolver] class, the user's body-less 'partial class X : IMessagePackFormatter<T>' appears to get no implementation and fails with CS0535. The requirement's example declares only the formatter.

This may fail RS2000 release-tracking checks, and the new IDs are unregistered. The diagnostics only fire on the new attribute, so existing users are unaffected unless they opt in.

hunches.claim: The generator's hand-written-formatter discovery excludes classes carrying GeneratedMessagePackFormatterAttribute by comparing a ToDisplayString to AttributeNamespace.AttributeName. Otherwise the same class would be registered twice, once as a custom formatter and once as ObjectSerializationInfo, and the resolver would contain a duplicate entry. If the comparison string is wrong (for example, the attribute namespace is 'MessagePack'), the exclusion silently fails and the resolver output changes.

receipt_plan.detail: Run the generator snapshot tests with a [GeneratedMessagePackFormatter] class and verify the resolver lists the formatter exactly once.

hunches.claim: The surrogate mode's generated Serialize/Deserialize bypass the generated formatters' MessagePackSecurity depth tracking. The standard templates call options.Security.DepthStep(ref reader) and reader.Depth-- on Deserialize, but GetSurrogateConversionCode emits no DepthStep. It relies on the surrogate formatter to enforce MaximumObjectGraphDepth. If the surrogate resolves to a custom or non-generated formatter, this level of nesting is not counted, so the depth limit applied to untrusted data is weakened. Contractless mode keeps the standard templates, so only surrogate mode is affected.

receipt_plan.detail: Deserialize deeply nested data (for example a self-referencing type) through a formatter generated with SurrogateType, with MessagePackSecurity.UntrustedData and a small MaximumObjectGraphDepth. Check that the depth limit throws as it does with the standard template. Compare against a contractless generated formatter.

hunches.claim: If SurrogateType names a type that is not an INamedTypeSymbol (for example typeof(int[])), the transform's 'as INamedTypeSymbol' yields null. The formatter then silently falls back to contractless mode instead of reporting an invalid surrogate.

hunches.claim: The surrogate path emits `new DataType() { ... }` and `new Surrogate() { ... }` object initializers that assign every member. The collector never checks that init-only or required members are settable this way. Read-write is enforced only through IsPublicReadWrite, which accepts init accessors. This is a correctness issue with no direct security impact.

hunches.claim: suppressed by unconfirmed context entry: [L11] area=analyzer, generator: Types that come from a referenced assembly are deliberately not analysed and get no formatter from the compiling assembly. In `TypeCollector.CollectCore`, after the custom-formatter, enum and generic checks, a non-generic type whose symbol is metadata-only exits with a bare `if (type.Locations[0].IsInMetadata) { return; }` (TypeCollector.cs:367-370), so no MsgPack003/004/005 diagnostic and no generated formatter appear for it. The defining assembly owns validating and formatting its own types (rationale inferred: the code has no comment). A missing diagnostic or formatter for such a type is not a defect. (source: src/MessagePack.SourceGenerator/CodeAnalysis/TypeCollector.cs:367) (would-be finding: The new feature generates a formatter for a type declared in a referenced assembly. A context-free reviewer might flag this as contradicting TypeCollector's metadata-only skip. [L11] records that skip as deliberate for implicit collection, and the new explicit opt-in path via [GeneratedMessagePackFormatter] does not go through TypeCollector.CollectCore.)

receipt_plan.detail: [L11] Types from referenced assemblies are deliberately not analysed or formatted by implicit collection. The new path is explicit opt-in through GeneratedFormatterCollector, so L11 is not contradicted.

hunches.claim: suppressed by unconfirmed context entry: [L8] area=docs: Requiring the MessagePackObject annotation by default is intentional, to enforce explicitness. [L8] says requiring the annotation by default is intentional. The requirement's maintainer comment explicitly allows contractless for this opt-in attribute, so it is consistent.)

receipt_plan.detail: [L8] Annotation requirement is deliberate for the default path. The attribute is an explicit opt-in, and REQ-2129 specifies contractless behaviour for it.

narrative: This run reviews reading B of REQ-2129 on branch review/ju26-issue-2129/B: Add [GeneratedMessagePackFormatter] with an optional SurrogateType property, where a user-defined surrogate type in Project B mirrors T's shape and keys are mapped by property name, so attribute-based keys and Union settings can be supplied without touching Project A. Code: Attribute has a SurrogateType property; generator reads keys/union attributes from the surrogate and emits conversion code between T and the surrogate, which the contractless-only reading would not do. As built on the branch: SurrogateType now makes the generated formatter copy T into a [MessagePackObject] surrogate and back, matching members by name, and delegate to the surrogate's own formatter so its keys and other attributes apply; contractless default unchanged
